Why your advisor asks how much you could lose and when you need the money

A plain-language guide to the two questions behind every investment risk profile in Canada—your willingness to accept losses and your ability to absorb them—with a stress test of five stock-and-bond mixes. Four charts and an editable scenario.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

"Recovers" means the account is back to the amount invested. The central idea

Your risk profile should reflect the lower of two answers: how big a drop you are willing to sit through, and how big a drop your plans can absorb before you need the money. A portfolio that passes only one test is too risky.

01

Two different questions: will you, and can you?

When you open an investment account in Canada, your advisor must work out your risk profile before recommending anything. Canadian securities regulators describe it as two separate factors. Risk tolerance is your willingness to accept risk—how you feel about seeing your account fall. Risk capacity is your ability to endure a financial loss—a more objective look at what a loss would actually do to you, given your income, savings, debts and when you need the money.

The two often disagree. A confident investor saving for a home purchase next year may be comfortable with swings but have little room for them. A nervous investor with a secure pension and 25 years until retirement may have plenty of capacity but little appetite. Regulators expect both to be asked separately, and say your overall risk profile should reflect the lower of the two unless the reason for anything else is documented.

02

A stress test: one bad year, then steady markets

The interactive model invests CAD 100,000 in five mixes, from 20% stocks to 100% stocks, with the rest in bonds. In the first year stocks fall 35% and bonds gain 2%. Afterwards stocks earn 7% a year and bonds 3.5%, and each mix is rebalanced annually. These are assumptions you can change, not a forecast or a replay of any historical period.

The first-year losses grow with the stock share: CAD 5,400 at 20% stocks, CAD 12,800 at 40%, CAD 20,200 at 60%, CAD 27,600 at 80% and CAD 35,000 at 100%. If the largest one-year drop you could live with is 15%—CAD 15,000—only the 20% and 40% mixes stay inside your limit. That answers the willingness question.

03

How long the money can wait decides the second answer

A loss you can wait out is different from a loss you must realize. In the same scenario the 20% mix is back to CAD 100,000 after 3 years, the 40% mix after 4, the 60% mix after 6, the 80% mix after 7 and the all-stock mix after 8. If you need the money in 5 years, only mixes up to 40% stocks recover in time. At year 5 the 60% mix would be worth about CAD 99,234 and the all-stock mix about CAD 85,202—below what you put in, exactly when you need it.

Here both tests point to 40% stocks, so the lower of the two is 40%. Change the inputs: with a 25% loss limit the willingness test allows 60%, but a 5-year horizon still holds the profile to 40%. Extend the horizon to 10 years and the ability test allows every mix, so your willingness becomes the binding limit.

04

What else your advisor weighs

A real risk profile is broader than this two-number test. Regulators expect advisors to assess capacity alongside your age and family situation, income, assets and debts, liquidity needs, investment objectives and time horizon, and to discuss and record any inconsistency—for example a high-risk answer from someone with limited savings who needs cash soon. Questionnaires help, but staff have criticised firms that relied on risk-tolerance questions alone or used generic labels without a clear method.

Expect to be asked to confirm the profile, and expect it to be updated when your life changes: a new job, a home purchase, retirement, an inheritance or a change in when you need the money can all change the answer.

05

How to use this before your next review

  • Write down the dollar drop—not the percentage—that would make you want to sell. Dollars are easier to picture.
  • Write down when you will need each part of the money. Money for next year and money for retirement may belong in different mixes.
  • Ask your advisor which of the two answers is limiting your profile today, and what would change it.
  • Remember that staying invested only helps if you can actually wait. The cost of selling in a bad year is shown in the year-5 chart.

This page explains concepts and does not assess your suitability. Your advisor's firm uses its own questionnaire, categories and limits.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Original stress-test illustration of generic 20%–100% stock mixes with reader-entered returns. Regulatory expectations from the December 2025 CSA/CIRO staff notice on client-focused reforms. No firm model portfolios, ratings or limits. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Joint CSA/CIRO Staff Notice 31-368 · Client Focused Reforms review (10 December 2025) ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026. Defines risk tolerance (willingness) and risk capacity (ability to endure loss), says the risk profile should reflect the lower of the two unless documented otherwise, and lists the KYC factors to assess with capacity.

  2. CSA · Client Focused Reforms frequently asked questions (December 2023) ↗

    Confirms that the risk profile consists of risk capacity and risk tolerance; also covers how costs are considered in suitability.
